rows.name: multipart-pause-1500
rows.question: For exactly ten thousand elements and one hundred ninety two threads per block, compute the minimum number of blocks needed to cover every element. Also report the active threads in the final block and the number of launched threads that need a bounds check. Explain the arithmetic.
rows.recognizedQuestion: For example, ten thousand elements and one hundred ninety two threads per block compute the minimum number of blocks needed to cover every element Also report the active threads in the final block and the number of launched threads that need a bounce check Explain the arithmetic
rows.answer:
You need 53 blocks, with 16 active threads in the final block and 176 excess threads that must be excluded by a bounds check—I’m interpreting “bounce check” as “bounds check.”

The arithmetic is 10,000 ÷ 192 = 52 full blocks with 16 elements left over, since 52 × 192 = 9,984, so we round up to 53 blocks. Those blocks launch 53 × 192 = 10,176 threads, leaving 10,176 − 10,000 = 176 threads outside the valid range. With the usual guard, `if (idx < 10000)`, all 10,176 launched threads evaluate the bounds check; 10,000 pass and 176 fail.

rows.name: switch-topic
rows.question: Switch topics. Why does snapshot isolation permit write skew even if both read-check-write sequences run in atomic transactions?
rows.recognizedQuestion: Switch topics. Why does snapshot isolation permit write skew even if both read-check-write sequences run in atomic transactions?
rows.answer:
Snapshot isolation permits write skew because atomicity makes each transaction all-or-nothing, but does not make concurrent transactions execute as if they were serial. Each transaction can check the same invariant against its own snapshot, then update different rows without triggering a write-write conflict.

For example, Alice and Bob are both on call, and at least one must remain on call. Two concurrent transactions each read that both are on call; one takes Alice off call, while the other takes Bob off call. Under snapshot isolation, both can commit because they write different rows, leaving nobody on call—even though each transaction’s check passed.

Serializable isolation prevents this outcome by rejecting or serializing the conflicting transactions. Another approach is to make both transactions lock or update a shared guard row before checking the invariant, with appropriate retry handling.
